 Loans Nearly 40% of Gen Z says debt is delaying homeownership
 Boomers feel shame and stress about financial woes, according to a survey by Accredited Debt Relief.
 Published Tue, Nov 3 2026 Dan Avery Updates editor, CNBC Select Share Share Article via Facebook Share Article via Twitter Share Article via LinkedIn Share Article via Email This article was paid for by Accredited Debt Relief . 
 Debt affects Americans at every stage of life, but its impact on their financial options varies by age, according to a new survey from Accredited Debt Relief , in partnership with Money.com. 
 Thirty-eight percent of Gen Z participants said debt was keeping them from saving for or buying a home, according to the survey, which included responses from 2,000 U.S. adults who carried debt over the past 12 months.

 Overall, 45% of Gen Z, defined as ages 18 to 29, said their debt load had increased over the past 12 months, the highest share of any generation in the survey. Additionally, nearly six in 10 said they frequently or constantly feel stressed about their financial obligations. 
"Financial debt is often stacked against you in your 20s," said Bobbi Rebell, chief financial education advisor at Accredited Debt Relief . "You have all these startup costs and you're not in your maximum earning years yet. So it's legitimately just tougher for anyone at that age."
 But certain pressures are making it harder for Gen Z than their predecessors, Rebell added.
"Student loan debt has increased proportionally. [Mortgage] rates, on a relative basis, are much higher," she said. "There are a lot of people sitting in their homes with 3% mortgages and now the rate is above 7%. That's just math."
For decades, homeownership has been viewed as the backbone of financial success. Rebell encourages young people, especially those struggling with debt, to think seriously about whether it's the path for them. 
 It's OK to enjoy the freedom of renting, she added, but you should still think about your financial future. Consider putting the money you would have allocated toward a home in investments. 
"The important thing for me, as a financial adviser, is to help people identify what they want and not worry so much about what other people say," she said. "And, by the way, it's okay to change your mind."
 How Gen Z can tackle debt 
 Starting your adult life with serious debt can make financial freedom seem impossible. In fact, less than 30% of Gen Zers in the survey said they feel optimistic about paying off their debt. 
 But there are a variety of strategies to get you back on track, no matter your situation.
 1. Make a budget. Putting a budget together doesn't necessarily mean depriving yourself — it's more about getting a clearer idea of where your money is going. Once you have that, you can decide what, if anything, you want to cut back on. In the Accredited Debt Relief survey, for example, 55% of respondents said they pared down on eating out, while 42% spent less on clothing and personal care items.
 2. Avoid lifestyle creep . "There is more pressure among Gen Z to live a 'better lifestyle' than in previous generations, because they see it more with social media," Rebell said. "It's supersizing the visibility of the things and experiences they want — even if the reality is they're rented or fake."
 3. Pay down your bills with the debt snowball or avalanche method. If you're able to make the minimum monthly payments on your credit card bills, the debt avalanche method can help you tackle your debts. You pay the minimums on all accounts and put all extra money toward the bill with the highest APR. Once that is paid off, you move to the next highest rate.  
 It saves you the most on interest and can get you debt-free faster. 
 If you need to see progress to remain motivated, though, adopt the debt snowball method. You pay the minimum on your cards, and throw all extra cash at the smallest balance. Once it's paid off, you move on to the next smallest balance. 
The snowball method costs you a little more in interest and takes slightly longer, but those quick early victories can build the momentum you need to stick with the plan
 4. Apply for a debt consolidation loan . A debt consolidation loan can allow you to swap several high-interest bills for one monthly payment with a lower fixed APR. Some lenders will even pay off your existing creditors directly.

 5. Work with a debt settlement company : If you're not able to make your monthly minimum payments, a debt settlement company might be a good option. They can negotiate with creditors to accept less than the full balance. However, only unsecured debts, like credit card bills and personal loans, can be enrolled. Mortgages, auto loans and other secured debts are ineligible. 
Fees associated with debt settlement vary by provider and state. Accredited Debt Relief says its success-based fees range from 15% to 25% of enrolled debt. 
 The company reports that clients who complete its program typically reduce eligible monthly payments by 40%.
